label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
reason: formatting, length, assistant talk or a placeholder
output:
Here's a draft. One note first: the reason you've been closing the laptop is that you've been trying to write it *in the right order* — move, then house, then feelings. It doesn't have to be in that order. I let it wander. It wanders into the kitchen about a third of the way in and that's where the good stuff is.

I kept it in your voice throughout — plain, a bit dry, funny in the places your Nana is actually funny. Swap the sign-off for whatever she calls you.

---

**Dear Nana,**

Two things before I start. First, I'm writing this on my laptop on a Thursday night, which means you're getting it on a Thursday too, just later, and Denise is going to be standing in your kitchen holding it, warning you it's long, that I'm not crying, and that it's fine. Second, I'm not going to try to write this in the right order, because that's the reason I've closed the laptop six times this week. It doesn't have to be in the right order. It just has to be true.

You're moving Saturday the 21st. Elmwood Terrace, second floor, a window that looks out at the parking lot and a big maple. I looked at the photos on their website more than I needed to. You said the room was "fine" and that the light was good in the mornings, which is you saying yes before you've said yes.

I'm going to say the one honest thing and then I'm going to leave it alone.

I wish I could be there Saturday. I'm on call all week and I couldn't swap out and I'm sorry. Not sorry about the job — sorry for you. You raised half the family in that kitchen and I don't think anybody should do that alone on a Saturday, not even you, and especially not when you're the one telling everybody else it's fine.

But here's what I keep coming back to: you did this. Nobody made you. Nobody dragged you off Kathleen Street. You picked the place, you signed the papers, you chose the second floor over the first for the maple and the parking lot. You did that at 88, which is more than a lot of people manage at 38 with a lot of help. My whole job is watching things that refuse to change because changing is scary and somebody has to be the one who pushes the button. You pushed the button. I'm proud of you for that. Not proud that you survived the move — proud that you did it yourself, on purpose, because you wanted a different thing for yourself.

Now. The house.

The house is 51 years of you, Nana. That's the thing I keep starting to say and then not saying. Grandpa Walt and you took it in 1974 and it stopped being a building a long time ago. It's a record of everything that happened in it. The kitchen is where half of our family exists. When I close my eyes I don't really see a kitchen, I see everybody in the kitchen.

Summers at the house. The deal was you dried the dishes and then you could stay up. I dried a *lot* of dishes. I got very fast at it, faster than any kid has a right to be, and you still made me redo the glasses because I was doing them too fast and you said a proper glass takes the same amount of time whether you're in a hurry or not. I thought that was the most ridiculous sentence anyone had ever said to a child. You were right, though. Everything you said was right, and I don't think you ever noticed that was a heavy thing to be handed at seven years old.

Then I'd sit on the floor in front of the little TV with the sound off, because it was too late to turn it up and I didn't want to wake anybody. You knew exactly where I was. You'd come in and stand in the doorway and say nothing about the score, you'd just hand me a glass of milk and go back to your chair. I remember thinking: she doesn't even care about the game. She cares that I'm in the room. I get it now, Nana. That was the whole thing. That was what it was about the whole time.

The back steps at 6am. I don't think you knew I was doing that. I'd come out in the dark and you'd be sitting there with your tea and you'd say good morning and then you wouldn't say another word until the cup was done. Not one word. Just the birds and the radio and the street. I used to think you were being kind, not saying anything, so I wouldn't feel like I had to talk. It wasn't that at all, was it. You just liked the quiet, and I was the only person up at 6am to have it with. Fifty-one years of 6am. I'm not going to be able to drink my tea in the morning without thinking about that, and I'm fairly sure that's fine.

You taught me crib when I was seven. Seven. And you never once let me win — not one single time, not even a little bit, not even when I was clearly close, which I frequently was and you frequently knew. I thought it was brutal. It wasn't brutal, it was *instruction*. I finally skunked you when I was fifteen and you got up and made me a whole pan of butter tarts, the ones with the crust you always cut too thick, and you set them on the counter and said that was for winning and not for being fifteen, and I want you to know I have never once in my life earned a better prize for anything. I still think about those tarts more than I'd like to admit.

I'm not going to write the next part as a eulogy for a house, because it's not one. But the house meant this to me: I knew where everything was. The good blanket, the batteries, the tea. It meant I could fall asleep on that couch and wake up and nobody would have asked me a single question. That's what 51 years does — it builds a place where you don't have to explain yourself. I've been looking for that my entire adult life, and I found a piece of it in a kitchen on Kathleen Street, and I got lucky. You gave me that. The house was the house, but you were the reason it worked.

Now, the card.

When I got the Toronto job, you put a $20 bill in an envelope, taped it to a card, and on the card you wrote: *for pizza, you look thin on the computer.* I've still got that card. It's in the junk drawer of my apartment and every time I find it I read it and laugh out loud by myself like an idiot. "Thin on the computer" doesn't even mean anything, Nana. It doesn't mean anything at all. And you got it exactly right anyway, which is the thing about you — you always got it exactly right, and it took you about a second and a half to do it.

The update you wanted: I eat better than I did in 2006. That's the headline. That's the whole story.

And last Christmas, my pager went off in the middle of dinner, and you said, "Is the internet broken again?" And I said no, Nana, it's a pager, it's for work, it doesn't mean anything's broken. And you said, "Well, can you fix it?" And I said no. And you said, "Hm." And then you went back to your dinner and let it go, which was honestly the most generous thing anybody could have done. But then I called you the next day and the first thing out of your mouth was "did anything break?" And it's every call now. Every single one. I answer it before you ask. Nothing broke, Nana. Nothing ever breaks. I check, every time, and then I call you back and tell you.

I'm glad you're still playing crib on Tuesdays with the church ladies, by the way. Eighty-eight years old and you're still beating people. The church ladies have no idea what they're up against and I'm not going to warn them. If anything, I want to see how it goes.

Grandpa Walt's been gone since 2019, and that house was built for two of you, and I don't think anybody says that out loud, but it's true. It got quiet in a way it wasn't supposed to get quiet. So no — you're not leaving something behind. You're going somewhere that fits you now. He'd have been the one telling you not to pack the good dishes, and then helping you pack them anyway.

Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I asked for the crib board, which means I'm the one hauling a crib board up to Toronto on a train in December like a lunatic. I want you to know I'm going to do it, and I'm going to complain about it the entire time, and it's going to end up in my apartment in a corner where I can see it. That clock is going to be ticking away in Denise's house and I hope she has the good sense to be frightened by it. Every hour. On the half hour it does the little thing with the little birds, and Dad used to time his showers to it.

And honestly? Elmwood looks good. It looks really good. They have a crib league, which I know you've been sitting on for a month waiting for a chance to mention, so — congratulations, you played it perfectly, drop it in wherever you want. You're going to walk in there and be the best crib player in that building inside six weeks and the church ladies are going to have to go find a new table.

Your window looks at the parking lot, which means you'll know every car that comes and goes — which, at your age, is basically the same as sitting out front, except in December nobody's going to make you shovel. Silver linings. I've been told that's the expression.

The thing about that maple is you're going to watch it all year. It does that thing where the leaves go yellow all at once and then there's nothing left for six weeks and it's just branches, and then in April it's green again and you'll be insufferable about it. I'm going to hear about that maple every single phone call until Christmas. I'm ready for it.

So here's the plan. December 5. I'm coming up the weekend the rotation's done. I'm bringing the crib board, and I'm going to set it up in your new second-floor apartment, and you and I are going to play the first game at Elmwood Terrace. Full rules. Your rules. The ones where I never win and you pretend you weren't stacking the deck. And if the church ladies want in, we can shuffle them in as a foursome and you can take all three of us apart, which you will, and I will enjoy watching.

So Elmwood Terrace, second floor, the first Saturday in December. Bring the cards. I mean it — pack the cards, don't let Denise put them in the cedar chest, I know what she's like with that cedar chest. Bring the cards and a deck I'll be able to hold in my hands, because I am not eighty-eight, even if I will be by the time you're done with me.

I'll bring the crib board and the butter tarts. Well, I'll bring the crib board. You'll have to make the tarts.

Happy almost-birthday-house, Nana. You did a hard thing and you did it by yourself, and I'd have given anything to be able to drive up and drive you down, and instead you're going to sit in your kitchen with a letter and Denise and a glass of something, and I hope it makes you cry a little, and I hope you laugh at the part about the parking lot, because that part's true.

And then December 5. Crib. Bring a card you haven't had to sneak past Denise for.

I love you more than the house did.

[Your name]

---

**P.S.** — Denise, if you're reading this out loud in the kitchen: read it like it was written. Don't tidy it up. Don't skip the pager part.

---

A few practical notes:

- **Print it on plain paper**, not cardstock, and don't staple the pages — she'll be holding it in one hand with a drink in the other. Two pages of regular paper with a fold is right; it feels like a letter instead of a certificate.
- **Let her have it before Denise reads it**, if you can. If Denise reads it and Nana's reaction happens secondhand, you'll lose the best part. If that's not possible, ask Denise to wait and hand it over first, then read it.
- **The first laugh is the $20 card** and the second is the parking lot/shoveling line — those are both grounded in things she actually said, so they'll land. The crib league one is your insurance policy if she's nervous rather than emotional.
